hints: Look closely at the CH2OH groups on each glucose ring. Do they all point the same way, or does every second ring look flipped upside down?
Remember how alpha-glucose (all the same way up) gives 1,4 links for starch, while beta-glucose (alternately flipped) gives 1,4 links for cellulose.
walkthrough:
**Spot the orientation clue**

Look at the four glucose rings from left to right. The CH2OH group is down, then up, then down, then up. That alternating pattern tells you every second monomer is rotated 180 degrees.

This is the classic signature of beta-glucose, not alpha-glucose.

**Name the linkage and the polysaccharide**

The rings are joined C1 to C4 by glycosidic bonds, so these are beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

Long, unbranched chains of beta-glucose joined by beta-1,4 bonds form cellulose.

**Link structure to function**

Beta-1,4 chains stay straight and line up side by side. They form many hydrogen bonds between chains to make strong fibrils and fibres.

That gives high tensile strength, perfect for supporting plant cell walls, so B is the correct description.

options.A: This describes amylose (and amylopectin/glycogen) made of alpha-glucose, which coils into a compact helix for storage, not the straight beta-glucose chain shown.
options.B: Correct. The alternating beta-glucose units form straight cellulose chains that bundle into fibrils with great tensile strength in plant cell walls.
options.C: Cellulose is fibrous and insoluble, not globular and soluble. A globular, soluble shape is not formed by these long straight beta-1,4 chains.
options.D: Cell markers are glycoproteins and glycolipids with short branched carbohydrate chains, not the long structural cellulose polysaccharide shown here.
